title: The light fades
hookLine: Anuruddha and his friends lose their inner light; doubt, inattention, fear and more

lines: THREE FRIENDS, LIKE MILK AND WATER.
cards: The hundred and twenty-eighth discourse opens with the Kosambi quarrel, the monks stabbing each other with words. The Buddha tries to make peace, and leaves.
He walks alone, and reaches a bamboo park where three monks live: Anuruddha, Nandiya and Kimbila, the ones who live together like milk and water.
Whoever comes back first sets out the seats; whoever sees the water pot empty fills it. Then Anuruddha admits a problem. When we meditate, he says, a light appears, and visions.
Then it fades, and we don't know why.

teach.b: The Buddha doesn't say the light was nothing. I had this too, he says, before my awakening. I saw light and forms, and they faded, and I had to find out why.
Then he lists what he found, the imperfections of the mind, upakkilesa, one at a time.
Doubt arose, and the light went. Inattention, and it went. Sleepiness and dullness.
Fear, like a traveler who suddenly sees killers jump out on both sides of the road. Elation, like someone looking for one way into a hidden treasure who suddenly finds five. Inertia in the body.

teach.h: THE QUAIL: TOO TIGHT, TOO LOOSE
teach.b: Too much energy, like gripping a quail too tightly in your hand: it dies. Too little, like holding it too loosely: it flies away.

teach.h: NAME IT, AND IT CAN BE LEFT
teach.b: Then longing. Then seeing too many different things. Then staring too hard at forms.

Each time, he understood: this imperfection arose, my stillness fell away, and the light faded. And each time he resolved: I won't let that arise again. The discourse isn't telling anyone to chase lights.
It teaches that when something good fades, there's usually a reason, and the reason can be named. Effort balanced like a hand that neither crushes nor drops the quail.

how: Some meditation teachers use the quail simile from MN 128 to describe balanced effort, and students in several traditions learn to notice and name hindrances such as doubt and dullness when concentration falls away.

o: a rule broken by a quarreling monk
a bright vision that proves you're awakened
an imperfection that clouds and dims the mind

games.q: why the light fades: tap the pairs.
p: one way to treasure, then five

s: the Buddha tells Anuruddha the light was imaginary
he says he had it too before his awakening, and teaches why it fades.
from doubt and inattention to effort too tight or too loose and staring too hard at forms.
the three friends quarrel at the start of MN 128
the quarrel is among the monks at Kosambi; Anuruddha, Nandiya and Kimbila live in harmony.

games.q: you're holding a quail in your hand. how should you hold it, in the Buddha's picture of effort?
o: neither too tight nor too loose.
games.why: too tight and it dies; too loose and it flies away. balanced effort is the hand that holds it just right.

practice: Think back to a recent moment when you felt clear or bright, and then it went, and ask what came in just before: doubt, hurry, gripping too tight, holding too loose. Name it quietly, without blame.
Then hold the breath the way the quail should be held: not crushed, not dropped.

wordCard.voice: Upakkilesa. Imperfections of the mind: the Buddha tells Anuruddha the inner light fades because of them, like doubt, fear and effort held too tight or too loose, and each can be named.

orig.note: Pali upakkilesa: imperfection, a defilement of the mind. the title of MN 128.

carryVoice: Your line: a quail held just right. Not crushed, not dropped. Day four ninety-six, done.
